tagline: A dirt loop into the last mountains put on the map.
intro: From Hanksville the loop leaves the desert floor and climbs into the Henry Mountains on a single lane of dirt, through badlands and buttes, canyons and cliffs, then up slopes of ponderosa and spruce to the alpine country of Bull Creek Pass. By the top it has climbed nearly a mile.

These were the last mountains in the lower 48 to be added to the map, in 1872, and the Navajo name for them means mountain whose name is missing. About 350 bison roam them now, descended from 18 animals brought down from Yellowstone in 1941.

moments.title: Eagle City
moments.text: A gold camp of about 1890 in Bromide Basin, almost empty by the First World War, where Frank Lawler stayed on alone for 60 years hunting the Lost Josephine Mine.

moments.title: Bull Creek Pass
moments.text: Past the spruce and ponderosa the road reaches alpine height, in mountains shared by mule deer, bighorn sheep, mountain lions and bison.

moments.title: Mount Ellen
moments.text: Almon Thompson climbed it in June 1872 and named it for his wife, and in 1895 Army signalmen flashed heliograph messages 183 miles from its summit to Colorado.

practical: A single-lane dirt road of 68 miles with rough sections, steep grades and blind curves. The BLM allows 6 to 8 hours, and Visit Utah advises nothing short of a stout, high-clearance vehicle.

sources.label: BLM, Bull Creek Pass Back Country Byway
